slides.title: Introduction to OOP
slides.content:
# Object-Oriented Programming 🏗️

OOP is a programming paradigm based on **objects** that contain data and code.

## What you'll learn:
- **Classes & Objects** - Blueprints and instances
- **Encapsulation** - Bundling data and methods
- **Inheritance** - Reuse and extend functionality
- **Polymorphism** - Same interface, different behavior
- **Multiple Inheritance** - Inherit from multiple classes
- **Operator Overloading** - Customize operators
- **Abstract Classes** - Define interfaces
- **Dataclasses** - Simplified class syntax

## Why OOP?
- 🧩 **Modularity** - Break down complex systems
- 🔄 **Reusability** - Don't repeat yourself (DRY)
- 🔒 **Encapsulation** - Hide implementation details
- 📐 **Abstraction** - Simplify complex reality
- 🐛 **Easier Debugging** - Isolated, testable units

> 💡 **Fun Fact:** Python is a "multi-paradigm" language - you can do OOP, functional programming, or procedural programming!

Let's build something great!

slides.title: Classes and Objects
slides.content:
# Classes & Objects 📦

A **class** is a blueprint; an **object** is an instance of that blueprint.

## Defining a Class

```python
class Dog:
    # Class attribute (shared by all instances)
    species = "Canis familiaris"
    
    # Constructor (initializer)
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        # Instance attributes
        self.name = name
        self.age = age
    
    # Instance method
    def bark(self):
        return f"{self.name} says Woof!"
    
    # String representation
    def __str__(self):
        return f"Dog({self.name}, {self.age})"
```

## Creating Objects

```python
# Create instances
buddy = Dog("Buddy", 3)
max_dog = Dog("Max", 5)

# Access attributes and methods
print(buddy.name)       # "Buddy"
print(buddy.bark())     # "Buddy says Woof!"
print(buddy.species)    # "Canis familiaris"
print(buddy)            # "Dog(Buddy, 3)"
```

## The `self` Parameter

- `self` refers to the **current instance**
- Must be first parameter in all instance methods
- Python passes it automatically when calling methods

> 💡 **Note:** `self` is a convention, not a keyword. You could use any name, but always use `self`!

slides.title: Instance vs Class Attributes
slides.content:
# Attributes Deep Dive 🔍

## Instance Attributes

Unique to each object.

```python
class Person:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name  # Different for each person

alice = Person("Alice")
bob = Person("Bob")
print(alice.name)  # "Alice"
print(bob.name)    # "Bob"
```

## Class Attributes

Shared by all instances.

```python
class Counter:
    count = 0  # Class attribute
    
    def __init__(self):
        Counter.count += 1
        self.id = Counter.count

c1 = Counter()
c2 = Counter()
c3 = Counter()
print(Counter.count)  # 3
print(c1.id, c2.id, c3.id)  # 1 2 3
```

## Method Types

```python
class MyClass:
    class_attr = "I'm shared"
    
    def instance_method(self):
        return f"Instance: {self}"
    
    @classmethod
    def class_method(cls):
        return f"Class: {cls.class_attr}"
    
    @staticmethod
    def static_method():
        return "I'm just a regular function"

obj = MyClass()
print(obj.instance_method())    # Uses self
print(MyClass.class_method())   # Uses cls
print(MyClass.static_method())  # Standalone
```

slides.title: Encapsulation
slides.content:
# Encapsulation 🔐

**Encapsulation** bundles data and methods that operate on that data.

## Access Modifiers (Convention)

```python
class BankAccount:
    def __init__(self, balance):
        self.owner = "Public"      # Public
        self._balance = balance    # Protected (convention)
        self.__pin = "1234"        # Private (name mangling)
    
    def get_balance(self):
        return self._balance
    
    def deposit(self, amount):
        if amount > 0:
            self._balance += amount
            return True
        return False

account = BankAccount(1000)
print(account.owner)        # Works ✓
print(account._balance)     # Works (but shouldn't access)
# print(account.__pin)      # ❌ AttributeError!
print(account._BankAccount__pin)  # Works (name mangling)
```

## Properties (Pythonic Getters/Setters)

```python
class Person:
    def __init__(self, age):
        self._age = age
    
    @property
    def age(self):
        return self._age
    
    @age.setter
    def age(self, value):
        if value < 0:
            raise ValueError("Age can't be negative")
        self._age = value

p = Person(25)
print(p.age)  # Uses getter: 25
p.age = 30    # Uses setter
# p.age = -5  # Raises ValueError!
```

> 💡 **Python Philosophy:** "We're all consenting adults." Use `_` prefix convention, not strict access control.

slides.title: Inheritance
slides.content:
# Inheritance 🧬

**Inheritance** allows a class to reuse another class's attributes and methods.

## Basic Inheritance

```python
# Parent (Base) class
class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name
    
    def speak(self):
        return "Some sound"
    
    def move(self):
        return f"{self.name} is moving"

# Child (Derived) class
class Dog(Animal):
    def speak(self):  # Override parent method
        return f"{self.name} says Woof!"
    
    def fetch(self):  # New method
        return f"{self.name} fetches the ball!"

class Cat(Animal):
    def speak(self):
        return f"{self.name} says Meow!"

dog = Dog("Buddy")
cat = Cat("Whiskers")

print(dog.speak())  # "Buddy says Woof!"
print(cat.speak())  # "Whiskers says Meow!"
print(dog.move())   # "Buddy is moving" (inherited)
print(dog.fetch())  # "Buddy fetches the ball!"
```

## Using super()

```python
class Employee:
    def __init__(self, name, salary):
        self.name = name
        self.salary = salary

class Manager(Employee):
    def __init__(self, name, salary, department):
        super().__init__(name, salary)  # Call parent
        self.department = department

mgr = Manager("Alice", 80000, "Engineering")
```

# Operator Overloading ➕

Customize how operators work with your classes using **dunder** methods.

## Arithmetic Operators

```python
class Vector:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y
    
    def __add__(self, other):       # +
        return Vector(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y)
    
    def __sub__(self, other):       # -
        return Vector(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y)
    
    def __mul__(self, scalar):      # *
        return Vector(self.x * scalar, self.y * scalar)
    
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Vector({self.x}, {self.y})"

v1 = Vector(1, 2)
v2 = Vector(3, 4)

print(v1 + v2)  # Vector(4, 6)
print(v2 - v1)  # Vector(2, 2)
print(v1 * 3)   # Vector(3, 6)
```

## Common Dunder Methods

| Method | Operator/Function |
|--------|------------------|
| `__add__` | + |
| `__sub__` | - |
| `__mul__` | * |
| `__truediv__` | / |
| `__eq__` | == |
| `__lt__` | < |
| `__len__` | len() |
| `__str__` | str() |
| `__repr__` | repr() |

slides.title: More Magic Methods
slides.content:
# More Dunder Methods 🪄

## Comparison Operators

```python
class Product:
    def __init__(self, name, price):
        self.name = name
        self.price = price
    
    def __eq__(self, other):   # ==
        return self.price == other.price
    
    def __lt__(self, other):   # <
        return self.price < other.price
    
    def __le__(self, other):   # <=
        return self.price <= other.price

p1 = Product("A", 10)
p2 = Product("B", 20)
print(p1 < p2)   # True
print(p1 == p2)  # False
```

## Container Methods

```python
class Playlist:
    def __init__(self):
        self.songs = []
    
    def __len__(self):              # len()
        return len(self.songs)
    
    def __getitem__(self, index):   # playlist[0]
        return self.songs[index]
    
    def __setitem__(self, index, value):  # playlist[0] = x
        self.songs[index] = value
    
    def __contains__(self, song):   # 'song' in playlist
        return song in self.songs
    
    def __iter__(self):             # for song in playlist
        return iter(self.songs)
    
    def add(self, song):
        self.songs.append(song)

playlist = Playlist()
playlist.add("Song A")
playlist.add("Song B")

print(len(playlist))        # 2
print(playlist[0])          # "Song A"
print("Song A" in playlist) # True
```

slides.title: Abstract Classes
slides.content:
# Abstract Classes 📐

Enforce that child classes implement certain methods.

```python
from abc import ABC, abstractmethod

class Shape(ABC):  # Abstract Base Class
    @abstractmethod
    def area(self):
        """Calculate the area"""
        pass
    
    @abstractmethod
    def perimeter(self):
        """Calculate the perimeter"""
        pass
    
    def describe(self):  # Concrete method
        return f"I am a {self.__class__.__name__}"

# shape = Shape()  # ❌ Error! Can't instantiate

class Rectangle(Shape):
    def __init__(self, width, height):
        self.width = width
        self.height = height
    
    def area(self):  # Must implement
        return self.width * self.height
    
    def perimeter(self):  # Must implement
        return 2 * (self.width + self.height)

rect = Rectangle(4, 5)
print(rect.area())       # 20
print(rect.perimeter())  # 18
print(rect.describe())   # "I am a Rectangle"
```

## When to Use Abstract Classes

- ✅ Define a common interface for related classes
- ✅ Ensure child classes implement specific methods
- ✅ Create frameworks and libraries
- ✅ Prevent instantiation of incomplete classes

> 💡 **Tip:** Use abstract classes when you want to define "what" but not "how".

slides.title: Dataclasses
slides.content:
# Dataclasses 📋

Simplified syntax for classes that mainly store data (Python 3.7+).

## Traditional Class

```python
class Person:
    def __init__(self, name, age, email):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age
        self.email = email
    
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Person(name={self.name!r}, age={self.age}, email={self.email!r})"
    
    def __eq__(self, other):
        return (self.name, self.age, self.email) == (other.name, other.age, other.email)
```

## With Dataclass

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Person:
    name: str
    age: int
    email: str
    # Auto-generates __init__, __repr__, __eq__!

p1 = Person("Alice", 25, "alice@email.com")
print(p1)  # Person(name='Alice', age=25, email='alice@email.com')
```

## Default Values and Field Options

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import List

@dataclass
class User:
    name: str
    email: str
    active: bool = True  # Default value
    tags: List[str] = field(default_factory=list)  # Mutable default
    
@dataclass(frozen=True)  # Immutable!
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int

point = Point(1, 2)
# point.x = 3  # ❌ FrozenInstanceError!
```

> 🎯 **Use Dataclasses** when your class is mainly for storing data. Use regular classes for complex behavior.

slides.title: Composition vs Inheritance
slides.content:
# Composition vs Inheritance 🧱

## Inheritance ("is-a" relationship)

```python
class Animal:
    def eat(self):
        print("Eating...")

class Dog(Animal):  # Dog IS AN Animal
    def bark(self):
        print("Woof!")
```

## Composition ("has-a" relationship)

```python
class Engine:
    def start(self):
        print("Engine started")
    
    def stop(self):
        print("Engine stopped")

class Car:  # Car HAS AN Engine
    def __init__(self):
        self.engine = Engine()
    
    def start(self):
        self.engine.start()
        print("Car is ready!")

car = Car()
car.start()
# Engine started
# Car is ready!
```

## When to Use Which?

**Inheritance:**
- When there's a true "is-a" relationship
- When you need polymorphism
- When base class is stable and unlikely to change

**Composition (Preferred!):**
- More flexible - easily swap components
- Avoids deep inheritance hierarchies
- Better encapsulation
- Easier to test

> 💡 **Golden Rule:** "Favor composition over inheritance" - Gang of Four

slides.title: Summary
slides.content:
# Amazing Work! 🎉

You've mastered Object-Oriented Programming in Python!

## Core Concepts
- ✅ Classes and Objects
- ✅ `__init__` constructor and `self`
- ✅ Instance vs Class attributes
- ✅ @classmethod and @staticmethod

## Four Pillars of OOP
- ✅ **Encapsulation** - Properties and access control
- ✅ **Inheritance** - super() and method overriding
- ✅ **Polymorphism** - Duck typing
- ✅ **Abstraction** - Abstract base classes

## Advanced Topics
- ✅ Multiple Inheritance & MRO
- ✅ Operator Overloading (dunder methods)
- ✅ Dataclasses for simpler syntax
- ✅ Composition vs Inheritance
- ✅ Design Patterns (Singleton, Factory, Builder)

## Best Practices
- 💡 Favor composition over inheritance
- 💡 Use dataclasses for data containers
- 💡 Keep classes focused (Single Responsibility)
- 💡 Use abstract classes for interfaces

> 🚀 **Challenge:** Build a library system with Book, User, Library classes, using inheritance and composition!
